--- Page 1 ---
ASTOR: Benchmarking and Improving
Autoformulation for Soft-Constraint Optimization
with a Formal Grammar
Amer Goel, Yeganeh Alimohammadi, Andrew Daw
Data Sciences and Operations
Marshall School of Business
University of Southern California
Abstract
Real-world decision problems combine two qualitatively different kinds of con-
straints: requirements that must be satisfied, called hard constraints, and preferences
that can be violated, called soft constraints. Because these problems are often posed
to decision-makers in natural language, large language models offer a natural tool
for assisting with their solution. This has given rise to autoformulation, which
focuses on using LLMs to translate natural-language descriptions of decision prob-
lems into executable mathematical optimization models. However, this research
often neglects soft constraints like those proposed by consumers, managers, and
planners, despite the fact that many practical problems require modeling them
explicitly. We introduce ASTOR, an inference-time framework that maps a natural-
language decision problem to a grammar-guided abstract syntax tree (AST) before
deterministically compiling the resulting representation into executable optimiza-
tion code. We also introduce SoftOR, a unified benchmark of natural language
problems which focuses on soft constraint formulations. On SoftOR, ASTOR
achieves the best aggregate accuracy among comparable single-request and multi-
agent LLM methods while remaining competitive on standard autoformulation
benchmarks that include only hard constraints. Code and data are available here.
1
Introduction
In practical settings, decision-makers often have to balance preferences from many stakeholders,
some of which are not always satisfiable. These preferences do not constrain their decisions the same
way that a strict requirement might. For example, a hospital manager must assign nurses to cover
every shift, but may accommodate preferences to avoid night shifts or maintain consecutive days off.
A travel agent must choose hotels and flights that obey the requested destination, but may not always
be able to accommodate brand preferences. A shopping agent must obey the consumer’s budget, but
may choose to suggest a longer delivery date than the one desired. An ideal optimization model must
therefore distinguish what must hold from what is preferred to hold, and when preferences conflict,
determine which take priority.
Natural language is a familiar way to express these distinctions, and the growing use of large language
models (LLMs) makes it an increasingly common interface for decision-making. Consumers use
AI tools for shopping and planning [Associated Press, 2025, Shopify, 2026, McKinsey & Company,
2026], while firms are incorporating AI for investments or as retail assistants [The Wall Street Journal,
2026, Reuters, 2026]. These settings often present decision-makers with hard and soft constraints.
As a result, LLM autoformulation provides a promising approach for this translation problem.
Research in this field often uses LLM prompting or fine-tuning methods to successfully translate
natural-language descriptions of real decision problems into solvable mathematical optimization
formulations. However, their methods often prioritize only hard formulations [Wei et al., 2022, Deng
Preprint.
arXiv:2610.26819v2  [cs.CL]  22 Oct 2026


--- Page 2 ---
et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2026] and current benchmarks only test those formulations [Ramamonjison
et al., 2022, AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024, Xiao et al., 2024, Huang et al., 2025a]. They do not
directly test whether a model distinguishes requirements from preferences or preserves the ordering
among preferences. This leaves an important class of practical decision problems without a strong
autoformulation method or evaluation tools.
We address this gap with ASTOR and SoftOR. ASTOR is an inference-time method which prompts
an LLM to express a decision problem as an abstract syntax tree generated by a formal grammar,
then validates and compiles that representation deterministically into solver code. The constructed
grammar is adequate for the class of hard and soft constraint optimization problems considered in this
work; see Appendix C. SoftOR is our newly introduced benchmark for evaluating whether models
can recover weighted-penalty and lexicographic soft-constraint formulations from natural language.
It consists of tasks involving travel planning and scheduling nurses for shifts in a hospital.
Across the 355 SoftOR instances, ASTOR achieves 88.5% solution accuracy, compared with 84.8%
for the strongest alternative. It achieves the highest accuracy on three of the four SoftOR datasets, with
the nurse scheduling dataset as the only exception. On 435 conventional hard-constraint problems,
ASTOR achieves 81.8%, within 0.5 percentage points of the best-performing method.
2
Related Work
Autoformulation. Autoformulation methods differ in both their output representation and their use of
inference-time computation. Under a single-request budget, Direct prompting returns a final solution,
Codegen produces an executable solver program, and Chain-of-Thought prompting generates a
natural-language derivation before producing the program [Deng et al., 2024, Wei et al., 2022, Yang
et al., 2026].
Other systems improve autoformulation by adding training supervision or iterative inference. ORLM
[Huang et al., 2025a] fine-tunes models on generated optimization instances, while LLMOPT [Jiang
et al., 2025] trains models to produce structured formulations before code generation. Chain-of-
Experts, OptiMUS, and ORThought instead distribute interpretation, formulation, implementation,
and correction across multiple agents or execution-conditioned stages [Xiao et al., 2024, AhmadiTesh-
nizi et al., 2024, Yang et al., 2026]. These methods demonstrate the value of additional supervision
and refinement. Some methods use intermediate representations to organize formulation or code
generation [Jiang et al., 2025, AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024], but these representations are often not
tailored to the task of optimization, nor do they admit any formal coverage guarantees. ASTOR uses
the inference budget of the single-request methods and a bespoke formal representation designed for
optimization formulations to produce more accurate models.
Benchmarking. Autoformulation benchmarks evaluate whether a system can translate a natural-
language problem into a solvable mathematical program. Early benchmarks focused on recovering
standard linear programs from relatively structured descriptions, as in NL4Opt [Ramamonjison et al.,
2022]. Later work expanded the task to longer descriptions, mixed-integer programs, executable
solver code, implicit constraints, and industrial problems [AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024, Huang et al.,
2025b, Xiao et al., 2024, Huang et al., 2025a, Yang et al., 2026]. Together, these benchmarks have
moved evaluation toward more realistic and structurally diverse formulation tasks [Xiao et al., 2025].
Evaluation methods differ by benchmark, but the most common kind is called solution accuracy
[Jiang et al., 2025, Yang et al., 2026, AhmadiTeshnizi et al., 2024, Xiao et al., 2024]. In this method,
each natural language instance is labeled a priori with a gold-standard optimal value that the authors
consider correct. This optimal value can be a number if there is a single objective function, or a vector
if there are multiple. To score an LLM autoformulation attempt, evaluators can take the optimization
model produced by an LLM for a single natural language instance, perform the optimization using a
solver like Gurobi, and compare the optimal value produced by the LLM’s optimization formulation
to the gold-standard value. The LLM’s attempt is scored as correct if and only if the optimal value
produced by its formulation matches the gold-standard value within the specified numerical tolerance.
Other methods use an LLM and graph methods like embedding distance or edit distance to score the
optimization formulation itself, instead of just the optimal value Liu et al. [2026], Zhang et al. [2026],
Abdul Rahman et al. [2026], Li et al. [2025], Wang et al. [2025]. This paper uses solution accuracy
as the primary evaluation metric, as well as some measures of formulation success.
Related benchmarks such as TravelPlanner, COMPASS, and SchedulingBenchmarks Nurse Rostering
contain requirements and preferences that may conflict [Xie et al., 2024, Qin et al., 2026, Curtois,
2


--- Page 3 ---
2014]. However, these are not well prepared for autoformulation benchmarking, because none jointly
provides complete natural language instances with gold-standard labeled optimal values. Additionally,
existing autoformulation benchmarks focus primarily on feasibility constraints and scalar objectives.
SoftOR is the first of its kind to directly target soft constraint formulations.
Formal Language in LLM Inference Formal languages have proven to be a useful intermediate step
in other LLM translation tasks. Researchers have defined bespoke formal languages to successfully aid
translation from natural language into formal logic or code, often representing the formulas produced
in those languages through tree-graphs called Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) [Aho et al., 2007, Alur
et al., 2013, Padhi et al., 2023]. For example, NL2LOGIC uses a Backus–Naur Form grammar
and AST representation to generate logical expressions that are translated into Boolean-solver code,
reporting up to 99% syntactic faithfulness [Putra et al., 2026]. AST-T5 and AST-based NL-to-
SQL methods likewise use syntactic structure to support code generation [Gong et al., 2024, Liao
et al., 2026], while AST-Probe finds recoverable code structure in language-model representations
[Hernández López et al., 2022].
Furthermore, the formal languages themselves often admit provable guarantees which are not ac-
cessible to other inference methods, and their computational representations as ASTs are useful for
downstream formal evaluation such as graph embedding and isomorphism [Li et al., 2025, Wang
et al., 2025]. These results motivate ASTs as an interface between language models and executable
formal systems, especially NL2LOGIC, which even uses ASTs for LLM translation and determin-
istic solving. ASTOR applies that interface to optimization and newly extends it to represent hard
constraints, weighted penalties, and lexicographic priorities.
3
Methodology
3.1
Formalizing Soft Preferences
Consider a user who specifies a collection of requirements and preferences over decisions x. We
represent each requirement as a hard constraint hj(x) ≤0, which every feasible solution must
satisfy, and each preference i with a nonnegative violation function vi(x), where vi(x) = 0 indicates
satisfaction and larger values indicate greater violation. The problem may also include a base
objective f0(x), such as monetary cost or total working time.
We consider two common formulations of these soft constraints:
lexicographic:
lex min
x
␀V1(x), . . . , VK(x), f0(x)


weighted penalty:

X

wi ≥0,
s.t. hj(x) ≤0.
In the lexicographic formulation, each soft constraint is assigned to one of K priority tiers by
Priority : N →N, with lower indices indicating higher priority. These are indices that denote
priority order in the mathematical formulation, operationally our method uses larger numbers to
denote higher ranks, which is equivalent. The aggregate violation Vk(x) sums the violations in
tier k. The objective then minimizes these tier violations in priority order, so an improvement at a
lower-priority tier cannot compensate for a loss at a higher-priority tier.
In the weighted-penalty formulation, each violation vi instead receives a nonnegative weight wi. The
weighted violations are added directly to the base objective, allowing preferences to trade off against
one another and against the original objective [Golden et al., 2024, Bärmann et al., 2025]. Both
formulations are common in goal-programming applications such as scheduling and planning.
3.2
Formal Grammar
The formal grammar G defines the intermediate language at the center of our method. G provides
compositional rules to assemble variables, domains, numbers, expressions, formulas, boolean connec-
tives, aggregations, and explicit priority levels into formulas that represent optimization models. This
grammar is given to our method as its output language, which guides it to create well-formed formulas
in a language we know to be well-suited for optimization with soft constraints. Other methods, which
3


--- Page 4 ---
output in natural language or solver-code, do not provide a bespoke formal representation designed
for a specific optimization task. Our method will do this through the use of a formal grammar.
However, the grammar used by our method does achieve one such guarantee. In particular, we use a
notion of adequacy, which is a standard notion in formal logic for establishing that a formal language
can represent its intended class of structures [Cheney et al., 2012, Otto, 2013]. In our case, G is
adequate for the class of optimization problems considered in this work when the correspondence
holds in both directions: every well-formed formula generated by G denotes a problem in the class,
and every problem in the class can be represented by a well-formed formula generated by G. Thus,
the grammar admits exactly the target problems without admitting any outside formulas [Cheney
et al., 2012, Otto, 2013]. Appendix C gives the complete grammar, formal definition, and proof.

Figure 1: ASTOR: One LLM call forms an AST which is compiled and solved deterministically.
Our method prompts an LLM with a natural-language problem and the grammar G to produce a
well-formed expression in the language generated by G, which in this case is an optimization problem
that may have hard or soft constraints. Every such expression admits a corresponding Abstract Syntax
Tree (AST), a tree-structured representation that makes the compositional relationships between
optimization components explicit. This gives our method a constrained intermediate representation
between natural language and executable optimization code. AST-based intermediate representations
have been used in natural-to-formal language translation to reduce generation errors and enforce
compositional consistency [Putra et al., 2026, Gong et al., 2024, Liao et al., 2026, Hernández López
et al., 2022]. We adapt this approach to mathematical optimization, and develop a typed grammar,
which is more expressive than some first-order-logic grammars developed in previous AST papers.
For this reason, we name our method ASTOR: Abstract Syntax Trees for Operations Research.
The specific implementation is in Figure 1. Concretely, the model is given a prompt including a
brief description of the task, the formal grammar, and a JSON schema which serializes the AST
and is the expected output form. The AST-JSON contains variable declarations, hard constraints,
soft constraints, and priority annotations. A deterministic post-processing pipeline applies only
local JSON repairs, validates and parses the resulting tree, and compiles it into executable Gurobi
code. Thus, the LLM is responsible for formulating the optimization problem, while all subsequent
translation from the formal representation to solver code is deterministic. The resulting solver output
is evaluated against the gold optimum. Worked examples and execution traces are provided in
Appendix B, with complete prompts and execution rules in Appendix D.
4
Building a New Benchmark: SoftOR
Existing LLM autoformulation benchmarks primarily evaluate feasibility and objective recovery for
problems expressed through hard constraints. Existing datasets contain preferences, but do not jointly
provide natural-language instances, verified gold optima, and annotations for both weighted-penalty
and lexicographic objectives. We therefore introduce SoftOR (Soft Operations Research), a unified
natural-language soft-constraint autoformulation benchmark covering both objective structures. To
construct and annotate lexicographic instances, we draw on the theory of modality from linguistics,
which studies expressions such as must, should, and may that describe necessity, obligation, and
desire [Henning et al., 2022, Garson, 2023]. These provide an immediate natural-language interface
for soft constraints, and linguistic theory already motivates an ordering on modal words by strength
that can be used to define lexicographic levels.
4


--- Page 5 ---
SoftOR comprises Nurse Rostering, COMPASS, TravelPlanner, and LexiBench. For the first three
components, we use published datasets as basic source material, but construct the natural-language
instances, soft-constraint semantics, priority annotations, and evaluation rules required for autoformu-
lation. LexiBench is entirely original. Table 1 summarizes the resulting components and identifies
the source data used in their construction.

4.1
Constructing New SoftOR Autoformulation Instances from Source data
The source data from Nurse Rostering, COMPASS, and TravelPlanner were designed for scheduling
or planning evaluation rather than natural-language optimization autoformulation and were therefore
not directly usable as SoftOR instances without our adaptations as described below.
For Nurse Rostering, we convert published tabular requirements into new natural-language instances
with explicit priority markers. Each published request weight becomes a fixed phrase. In particular,
the original priority markers, annotated as 1, 2, 3, and 100, become “slightly prefers," “prefers,"
“strongly prefers" and “far more serious." The original numbers are not kept in the final natural
language instance, since we intend to test whether these ordinal priorities can be recovered from
language alone. Optima are provided by the original benchmark authors [Curtois, 2014]. Numerical
weights are not given to any method. Each method instantiates its own weights, if it chooses to use
them, and the specific numerical weights given by the benchmark are used only post-modeling for
scoring and evaluation. We chose not to show weights to any route during decision-making so we can
evaluate each route’s ability to infer preference strength from natural language. As an ablation, we
run a case where routes can see weights before decisions in Appendix F.
The original COMPASS source material provided a natural-language query, structured hard constraints
and preferences, a finite set of candidate plans, and one annotated gold plan ID [Qin et al., 2026].
It did not present these elements as a single autoformulation instance or annotate the underlying
optimization objective. To adapt these instances for SoftOR, we combine the query and structured
fields into a complete natural-language problem using fixed templates that mark requirements as
"required" and wishes as equally important soft constraints that are "preferred". We also reconstruct
the gold objective. Because multiple plans may satisfy the same maximum number of preferences,
we enumerate every provided plan and use that maximum as gold rather than requiring the single
plan ID supplied originally by COMPASS.
The original TravelPlanner source already provided natural-language travel-planning problems and
structured candidate data, but it was designed to evaluate plan generation and does not supply
annotated optimization formulations or gold objective vectors [Xie et al., 2024]. For our adaptation,
we convert each instance into a lexicographic autoformulation task by assigning its linguistic cues to
three priority tiers. These cues, called modals, express obligation, intention, or desire, and the tiers
follow the deontic–teleological–bouletic distinction in modal linguistics [Rubinstein et al., 2013, von
Fintel and Iatridou, 2008, Portner, 2009, Henning et al., 2022]: deontic language states what must
hold, teleological language what the speaker plans to achieve, and bouletic language what the speaker
wants. We then enumerate every valid combination of transport, one hotel per city, and restaurants;
compare plans lexicographically by tier violations; and break ties by total cost. The resulting optimal
vector is the gold annotation, and a formulation is correct only if its solution matches that vector at
every tier and in cost. The complete inventory of linguistic cues and benchmark construction details
is included in Appendix F.
4.2
Original Construction of LexiBench
LexiBench is an original dataset of 75 problems that tests richer ordered preferences than the
preceding sources, which contain either fixed weights or at most three tiers. Figure 2 shows its five
preference structures. Each structure is instantiated for three decision types. Atomic problems select

Figure 2: Priority annotation in LexiBench instances. Arrows indicate priority ordering: left is a

one element from a candidate set, as in COMPASS. Assembly problems build a bundle from several
candidate sets, as in TravelPlanner. Constructive problems formulate constraints and optimize over
an implicitly defined feasible region, as in conventional hard-constraint benchmarks. Hardness is
signaled with the same modal cues as TravelPlanner, and when more than three levels are needed,
explicit comparatives such as “more important than,” “higher priority,” and “above all” fix the
remaining order. Gold is computed by enumeration for atomic and assembly problems and by solving
the annotated lexicographic model in Gurobi for constructive problems. A formulation is correct if it
attains the gold objective vector, regardless of which optimal solution it returns.
The priority signal column of Table 1 records how each source communicates priority, and Ap-
pendix A disaggregates accuracy by it. Explicit sources state priority in words that name a level
directly, such as “strongly prefer” and “slightly prefer” in Nurse Rostering or “equally important” in
COMPASS. Modal sources encode priority only through the modal verbs above, so the tier must be
inferred from the strength of the wording. Mixed sources, namely LexiBench, combine modal cues
with explicit comparatives and pairwise statements, so recovering the ordering requires both readings.
Appendix F gives the complete construction and annotation procedures for SoftOR.
5
Experiments
To evaluate ASTOR, we compare it with single-request prompting methods and previously published
agentic autoformulation methods across hard and soft constraint benchmarks. Our experiments
address the following research questions:
• RQ1: How accurately do single-request and multi-agent inference methods solve soft-constraint
benchmarks? How does this performance differ by lexicographic and weighted penalty objectives?
• RQ2: How does accuracy vary by priority signal and problem difficulty?
• RQ3: What technical and solution errors do the methods produce?
• RQ4: How expensive is ASTOR compared to other methods?
• RQ5: How do the ASTOR components and backbone affect performance?
5.1
Experimental Setup
For our main experiment, we evaluate on SoftOR using temperature-zero Gemini 3.7 Flash as the
LLM backbone with the provider-default thinking configuration on most benchmarks. The only
exception is Nurse Rostering, where all routes receive an increased thinking budget and use Gemini
3.8 Flash, due to its more complex formulations. Appendix A includes additional experiments on
standard autoformulation benchmarks distributed by Yang et al. [2026], but these include almost
exclusively hard constraints. A non-reasoning model, a non-Gemini reasoning model, and a larger
Gemini reasoning model are included in later ablation studies on SoftOR and standard benchmarks.
Solution Accuracy, as defined in Section 2, is the primary evaluation metric, and other metrics
are reported in Table 3 for more granularity on which soft constraints are most often satisfied.
Since lexicographic problems have multiple objectives, gold-standard labels are vectors, and LLM
formulations are considered correct if and only if the entire lexicographic objective vector produced
matches the gold-standard one within the specified numerical tolerance. Weighted-penalty problems
have a single objective, so the gold standard label is a number, and similarly, formulations are correct
if and only if the number produced matches the gold-standard value within the specified numerical
tolerance.
We compare against three single-request routes using the same backbone model. Direct is given
the natural language problem and predicts the final answer with no intermediate representation.
Code-generation (Codegen) is a single-request LLM prompting method which is given the natural
6


--- Page 7 ---
language problem and outputs executable Gurobi code to solve the problem [Deng et al., 2024]. This
is the main control of the experiment, and tests whether a formal grammar provides any advantage
over another formal intermediate representation, like solver code. Chain-of-Thought (CoT) asks the
LLM to think in steps to produce a mathematical optimization model and executable Gurobi code
[Wei et al., 2022]. ORThought uses agents to formulate the optimization problem as executable code
and at most three repair agents to debug the formulation or code [Yang et al., 2026]. Chain-of-Experts
(CoE) uses a panel of many LLM agents to collaborate on formulation, coding, and natural-language
extraction [Xiao et al., 2024]. ORThought and CoE use published prompts.
Direct, Codegen, and CoT are single-request LLM prompting methods, whereas CoE and ORThought
are multi-request pipelines that use different LLM prompts for formulation, repair, and execution. We
estimate sampling uncertainty with 10,000 paired bootstrap resamples over problem instances, using
the same sampled instances for every method. Tables report bootstrap standard errors in parentheses,
and figures show percentile 95% confidence intervals. Appendix D gives the prompts.
5.2
RQ1: Accuracy
Overall, ASTOR is the most accurate on SoftOR, with an aggregate accuracy across lexicographic
and weighted penalty problems of 88.5%. From most to least accurate, the baselines achieve 84.8%
for CoE, 83.7% for Codegen, 81.4% for CoT, 80.0% for ORThought, and 52.7% for Direct. We now
report results stratified by objective type (lexicographic or weighted), including more granular data
on soft constraint satisfaction.

5.2.2
Weighted Penalty Problems (Nurse Rostering Instances)
Table 4 shows the performance of each method on each instance of Nurse Rostering. Numbers
indicate incurred surplus penalty by violating staffing requirements or shift preferences. Zero penalty
is an optimal solution. FAIL denotes instances where the route failed to obey all hard constraints or
failed to produce a roster at all. Codegen and CoT are the most accurate on this dataset, with 9/15
correct instances (0 penalty). ASTOR and ORThought have 8/15, CoE has 7/15, and Direct has 0/15.
ASTOR is as good as all other inference methods on staffing measures. It is neither the worst nor the
best on weighted shift preferences. Details on Nurse Rostering are available in Appendix F.
5.3
RQ2: Performance by Problem Characteristics
Figure 4: Correct instances ordered by Direct
token usage as a proxy for difficulty.
We disaggregate results by difficulty level, with to-
ken usage as a proxy. Figure 4 has all 355 SoftOR
instances as its horizontal axis, ordered from least
to most token usage on the Direct route. Token us-
age counts how many tokens the Direct route used to
produce an answer for that instance. Each tally mark
indicates a correct answer for that instance. The sec-
tion on the right, called "Direct Failures" is for those
instances Direct did not produce a roster, and does
not have token ranks on its horizontal axis. In this
case, instances are sorted alphabetically by dataset
name and then instance ID, and tally marks indicate
correct solutions for each route. Figure 3a uses the
same definition of token usage, and aggregates them
into five roughly equal groups, called quintiles, with
Q1 containing the lowest token usage and Q5 the highest. ASTOR performs best, even as the difficulty
level of the problem increases. More disaggregated results are in Appendix A (Figure 6).
5.4
RQ3: Error Analysis
We analyze technical and solution errors as percentages of all evaluated attempts. Technical errors
include malformed outputs, parsing, compilation, or execution failures. Solution errors indicate that
the optimal value is different than the gold-standard. More details are in Appendix E.
ASTOR has the lowest error rate (i.e., percent of instances with either technical or solution errors) on
SoftOR among the compared methods (Figure 3b). The whiskers show 95% bootstrap confidence

intervals for the total error rate, combining technical and solution errors, and the unplotted remainder
up to 100% represents correct attempts. On LexiBench, Codegen and CoT often satisfy the right
preferences but fail to choose the cheapest solution among equally preferred options, accounting
for 5 of Codegen’s 8 solution errors and 10 of CoT’s 12. ASTOR instead gives up preferences to
reduce cost in five of its six errors because it combines preference penalties and cost in a weighted
sum. In the remaining case, it gives the highest priorities to the wishes the request explicitly says to
give up first. On the hard-constraint benchmarks, error rates are similar for ASTOR, Codegen, CoT,
ORThought, and CoE, for which full details are included in Appendix A.
5.5
RQ4: Cost Analysis
We report the incurred cost in USD of ASTOR and other methods at the time of evaluation. Figure 3c
shows ASTOR is 10.3% less expensive than CoE, the strongest alternative, while also being the most
accurate. Other cost results are in Appendix A, where ASTOR shows a similar profile.
5.6
RQ5: Ablation Studies
We examine the prompt components and LLM backbone of ASTOR. Following precedent for analysis
on fixed benchmark subsets [Song et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2025, Yao et al., 2025], we construct a frozen,
stratified 100-instance sample drawn from the eight benchmarks, including the four from SoftOR and
four hard-constraint-only benchmarks in Appendix A. All main-text ablations report results on the 45
soft-constraint instances included in the sample, while Appendix A reports the corresponding results
on the complementary 55 hard-constraint instances. For every ablation except the LLM backbone,
the same settings as the main experiment are applied to each dataset.
As seen in Appendix D, the ASTOR prompt has several components, and we remove one for each
ablation. The ASTOR prompt includes the formal grammar in two parts, one as a human-readable
markdown file in the style of a BNF grammar, and the other as a JSON schema that specifies the
expected form of the output. It also supplies a benchmark contract, with bespoke information needed
to use the data of each benchmark. Lastly, ASTOR uses a deterministic Python code repair which
detects and fixes syntax mistakes in the JSON output, for which more information is available in
Appendix A.

Figure 5: ASTOR prompt ablations on SoftOR. Whiskers show bootstrap 95% confidence intervals.
Removing the human-readable grammar and the deterministic repair reduced performance by only
2.2 and 4.4 percentage points, respectively, indicating that the serialized grammar may be enough and
that syntax errors are uncommon. Removing the benchmark contract reduces performance by more.
The last bar in Figure 5 gives the human grammar to the Direct method, provided as a tool for internal
reasoning only. This method performs exactly the same as the Direct method on the ablation set.

6
Discussion and Conclusion
SoftOR makes soft-constraint autoformulation measurable through weighted penalties, lexicographic
objectives, and solver-verified gold annotations, and ASTOR shows that a formal intermediate
language improves accuracy on exactly those problems, particularly ordered preferences, while
remaining competitive on hard constraints. Future work should define and evaluate on a metric of
faithfulness to the original optimization problem or solver performance and extend the benchmark
with less explicit language to test how well the method transfers to those settings. Overall, the results
support formal languages and ASTs as practical foundations for optimization autoformulation.
10


--- Page 11 ---
Ethics Statement
This work does not involve human subjects, personal data, or sensitive attributes, so institutional re-
view board approval was not required. SoftOR is built from publicly released benchmarks (COMPASS,
TravelPlanner, and SchedulingBenchmarks) under their original licenses, together with LexiBench,
an original dataset written and annotated by the authors. All priority annotations, gold constructions,
and error labels were produced by the authors following the protocols in Appendices E and F, and
no crowdsourcing or paid annotation was used. The natural-language instances describe scheduling,
travel, and staffing scenarios with fictional entities and contain no real individuals. Experiments call
commercial LLM APIs, and the available token usage and cost of every reported run are recorded in
Appendix A at the prices listed in Appendix D so that the environmental and financial footprint of the
study is visible. The methods and benchmark are intended to make optimization formulation more
faithful to stated preferences and carry no foreseeable dual-use risk beyond that of general-purpose
optimization tooling. The authors have no conflicts of interest or sponsorship to declare.
Reproducibility Statement
We release the complete ASTOR pipeline, the SoftOR benchmark with its gold annotations, all
prompts, and the raw outputs and evaluation records of every reported run as supplementary material
and at the repository linked in the abstract. The formal grammar, the definition of the problem class,
and the full proof of adequacy are in Appendix C, and Appendix B works one instance through
the pipeline with its literal compiler trace. Appendix D gives the exact prompts for the four single-
request routes, the configuration and prompt provenance of ORThought and CoE, the benchmark
contracts, the execution and evaluation rules, the frozen decoding and pricing settings, and the
ablation definitions. The identifiers of the frozen 100-instance ablation subset are available through
the repository. Appendix F documents every dataset adaptation, including the TravelPlanner priority
rules, the LexiBench construction, the Nurse Rostering phrase mapping, the COMPASS templates,
and the gold-label corrections applied to the ORThought releases. Section 5.1 states the backbone,
decoding settings, and bootstrap protocol, and Appendix E gives the error-labeling decision order.
AI Use Statement
In this work, we used generative AI tools to generate the natural-language instances of SoftOR by
applying a dataset-construction procedure that the authors designed without AI, to clean and reformat
source datasets, and to assist in the exposition of author-developed adequacy proofs in Appendix C,
but not with formulating the mathematical claims. It was also used to provide feedback on the
experimental design, and to implement the ablation experiments. We have not used generative AI
tools to develop the conceptual framework or the formal grammar, to propose or refine hypotheses, to
design the methodology, or to interpret results. Translation and qualitative or thematic analysis are
not applicable to this work. Additionally, we used generative AI tools to create and edit software code,
to create scientific figures, to brainstorm, to edit the paper for readability, and to format references.
We have reviewed all AI-assisted work. We take responsibility for the final content of this work,
including text, claims, and artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI.

Figure 6 disaggregates the hard-constraint benchmarks by formulation type and problem size for
hard constraints, and priority signal for soft constraints. Problem types are Linear Program (LP),
Integer Linear Program (ILP), Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP), and Nonlinear Program (NLP).

explicit, modal, or mixed markers for lexicographic formulations, and weighted penalty formulations
are always explicit. ASTOR leads on ILPs and on toy problems, and a different baseline leads in
each remaining category, and achieves the highest accuracy for every lexicographic signal, with its
largest margins when priorities are modal or mixed. Codegen and CoT tie for the highest accuracy on
weighted-penalty Nurse Rostering.

B
Worked Example
We use the following natural-language instance throughout. Blue marks the hard requirements and
query, red marks the soft preferences.
A ward manager is scheduling Alice for an 8-hour Day shift on any of Monday through Friday.
Wednesday is already an agreed fixed day off, and her contract requires her to work at least 16
hours this week. She strongly prefers to work Monday and Tuesday, and slightly prefers to
work Thursday. The manager would like to minimize the number of hours Alice works. Which
days should she work?
This appendix works the Nurse Rostering example through a compact view of the grammar, from
declarations to three finished models.
B.1
Simplified Grammar View
Figure 10 summarizes the compositional rules of an example grammar constructed for this problem.
The complete grammar for ASTOR appears in Appendix C. A program is a block of declarations
followed by a model, and a model is one objective together with a list of named constraints. Expres-
sions are built from constants, symbols and indexed symbols, combined with arithmetic operators, a
small set of functions, and aggregation over an index set. A formula either compares two expressions
or joins other formulas with the usual connectives.
The
objective
is
where
the
preferences
are
formalized,
and
it
has
three
forms.
Objective(feasibility) is a problem with nothing to optimize. Objective(sense, ⟨Expr⟩)
is a single scalar objective, which is the form a weighted-penalty model takes, since its penalty
terms are folded into that one expression. Objective(sense, ⟨Tier⟩,...) takes an ordered list of
tiers, each carrying its own expression, and a lexicographic model uses that form instead. This lets
18


--- Page 19 ---
an evaluator tell two formulations apart by looking at the tree, without going back to the natural
language.
⟨Program⟩::= ⟨Declarations⟩⟨Model⟩
⟨Declarations⟩::= Declarations(⟨Params⟩, ⟨Vars⟩)
⟨Params⟩::= Parameters( name : ⟨Const⟩, . . . )
⟨Vars⟩::= Variables(⟨Domain⟩, name, . . . )
⟨Domain⟩::= {0, 1} | Z | R | [low, hi]
⟨Model⟩::= Model(⟨Objective⟩, ⟨Constraints⟩)
⟨Objective⟩::= Objective(feasibility)
| Objective(sense, ⟨Expr⟩)
| Objective(sense, ⟨Tier⟩, . . . )
⟨Tier⟩::= priority(k, ⟨Expr⟩)
⟨Constraints⟩::= Constraints(⟨Constraint⟩, . . . )
⟨Constraint⟩::= name(⟨Formula⟩)
⟨Formula⟩::= ⟨Expr⟩▷◁⟨Expr⟩
| ¬P | P ∧Q | P ∨Q | P ⇒Q | P ⇔Q
⟨Expr⟩::= ⟨Term⟩| ⟨Expr⟩⊕⟨Expr⟩
| f(⟨Expr⟩, . . .) | agg v∈S ⟨Expr⟩
⟨Term⟩::= ⟨Const⟩| ⟨Sym⟩| ⟨Sym⟩[⟨Index⟩, . . .]
sense ∈{maximize, minimize}; ▷◁∈{≤, <, =,̸ =, >, ≥}; ⊕∈{+, −, ×, ∇·,ˆ}; f ∈{abs, min, max, exp, log,
sqrt}; agg ∈{P, Q, min, max, count}; P, Q range over ⟨Formula⟩.
Figure 10: An example grammar, which generates optimization problems that have hard constraints,
weighted-penalty objectives, or lexicographic preferences. Preferences are syntactically encoded.

Figure 12: Different formulations of the nurse problem. Formulation (a) contains no preferences, (b)
penalizes violations by scalar terms λ, µ chosen by an author, and (c) tiers the preferences based on
lexicographic strength, with the time objective as the final tie-breaker.
The optima differ as well. With no preferences stated, any two shifts that avoid Wednesday meet the
16-hour minimum, so the answer is not unique. Under the weighted objective at λ = 3 and µ = 1,
Alice works Monday and Tuesday: satisfying the Thursday request would cost eight more hours
to relieve one point of penalty, so the solver drops it. Under the lexicographic objective she works
Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, because hours only break ties among rosters that already satisfy
both request levels, and no saving in hours can outrank a request at a higher level.
A weighted model will trade a preference away once the objective pays enough for it, and a lexico-
graphic model will not.
20


--- Page 21 ---

LexiBench: habitat crew-days
Problem statement. Divide the season’s habitat-restoration crew-days among erosion control,
wetland repair, native planting, and trail improvement. The wish we would surrender last is that
at least 21 crew-days go jointly to erosion control and wetland repair; the others together do not
equal it. The season allows 29 crew-days in total, and weather rules out any extension. Ignore
how the days were split last season. Those remaining wishes are tied with one another and
rank below it: every one of the 29 available crew-days is put to use; at least 10 crew-days go to
native planting; and at least 10 crew-days go to trail improvement. Each site must receive at
least one crew-day. Allocations must be nonnegative whole numbers. Determine the allocation.

suppresses only serialization scaffolding such as repeated node-type labels, null defaults, expression
wrappers, descriptions, and copied source text. The JSON Schema and benchmark instance are

C
Formal Grammar and Its Adequacy
C.1
Complete Grammar
The complete abstract-syntax grammar used by ASTOR is given here. The suffixes X*, X?, X{n},
and X{n,} denote, respectively, zero or more occurrences, an optional occurrence, exactly n occur-
rences, and at least n occurrences. We read G as a typed grammar: symbol occurrences resolve to
declarations, operators are applied to arguments of the displayed sorts, penalty weights and violations
are nonnegative, and preference relations determine ordered priority tiers, allowing ties.

C.2
Soft-constraint Specifications
Soft-constraint semantics.
Each soft constraint has a condition: a true-or-false statement de-
scribing the desired outcome, such as “the hotel costs at most $100.” An optional guard is another
true-or-false statement that determines whether the preference applies, such as “the hotel is selected.”
Without a guard, the preference always applies.
For a solution x, the penalty vi(x) is zero if the guard is false. Otherwise, it is zero if the condition is
true and one if it is false. In weighted_sum mode, an optional violation expression can specify
the penalty instead. This expression must be nonnegative and zero exactly when the condition is true.
All soft constraints must specify the same aggregation mode. For weighted_sum, each must supply
a nonnegative weight that multiplies its penalty. Priorities are unused. For lexicographic, the
objective counts violated preferences within each tier, with each violated preference contributing one
regardless of its weight or violation expression. Tiers with larger priorities are optimized first. Every
constraint’s tier must be specified explicitly or fully determined by preference relations. No default
priority is assumed.
C.3
Representational Adequacy
Let O be the class of finite optimization problems over binary, integer, real, bounded, or finite
categorical decision domains. Hard constraints and objectives are formed by finite compositions of
constants, indexed quantities, arithmetic and elementary functions, norms, conditionals, piecewise-
linear functions, finite aggregations, comparisons, Boolean connectives, and quantification over finite
index sets. A problem may additionally contain nonnegative soft-constraint violations combined by
either weighted penalties or a finite lexicographic priority ordering.
A sort is the type of value represented by a node, such as an integer, real number, Boolean value,
string, or element of a declared finite set. An AST is well-sorted when every operation is applied
to inputs of the appropriate types. For example, arithmetic operations require numeric inputs, a
comparison of two numeric expressions produces a Boolean-valued condition, and a quantified
index must range over a declared finite set. An AST is well-formed if its construction does not
contradict the rules of G and if all references and indices are valid, expressions and aggregations are
defined wherever evaluated, piecewise constructions are unambiguous, and priority annotations and
relations determine ordered tiers for all soft constraints, allowing ties. A partial ordering that leaves a
constraint’s tier unresolved is insufficient.
Let A be the set of well-formed, well-sorted ASTs generated by G. The grammar defines a map
J·K : A −→O.
For an AST A, JAK is the optimization problem described by A: its decision domain, feasible set,
and ordering of feasible solutions. This map is evaluated recursively, with each node applying its
specified operation to the meanings of its children.
We consider two optimization problems equivalent if they have the same decision domain and feasible
set and rank all feasible solutions in the same order. For this representation, adequacy means that the
semantic image of G is exactly O: the grammar represents all and only the problems in the target
class [Cheney et al., 2012, Otto, 2013]. The following results prove the two set inclusions.
Lemma C.1 (Representation of expressions and conditions). Every Expr generated by G is a well-
sorted term, and every Formula generated by G evaluates to either true or false. Conversely, every
expression and condition allowed in a problem in O can be represented by an Expr or Formula in G.
The original and represented versions return the same value or truth value for every valid assignment
of the decision variables and data.
24


--- Page 25 ---
Proof. For the forward direction, we use induction over the nodes of a well-formed AST generated
by G, proceeding from the leaves to the root.
Base case.
A leaf is a constant, symbol, or indexed_symbol. A constant has its stated value
and sort; a symbol or indexed_symbol inherits the sort of its declaration. Since G requires symbols
and indices to agree with their declarations, every leaf is well-sorted.
Inductive step.
The inductive hypothesis is that every child Expr or DataExpr is well-sorted and
every child Formula or DataFormula is Boolean-valued. Proceeding to the parent, an operation
applies a typed operator to compatible expressions; a conditional selects between compatible branches
using a Boolean condition; and an aggregation combines well-sorted values over a declared finite
domain. A comparison, membership, logical, or quantifier node returns a Boolean value
when applied to children of the required sorts. By the inductive hypothesis and the typing requirements
of G, the parent is therefore well-sorted if it is an expression and Boolean-valued if it is a formula.
This completes the induction.
For the converse direction, we use induction over the nodes of any expression or condition allowed in
a problem in O.
Base case.
A leaf is a constant, scalar quantity, or indexed quantity. It is represented by a constant,
symbol, or indexed_symbol node, respectively, with the same value and sort.
Inductive step.
The inductive hypothesis is that every child has a representation in G returning
the same value or truth value on every valid assignment. Proceeding to the parent, arithmetic and
elementary functions, norms, and conditionals are represented by operation; finite aggregations by
aggregation; piecewise-linear expressions by Piecewise; comparisons and membership condi-
tions by their corresponding Formula productions; Boolean combinations by logical; and finite
universal or existential conditions by quantifier. Data-only constructions use the corresponding
DataExpr and DataFormula productions. By the inductive hypothesis, the represented children
agree with the original children; because the parent applies the same operation, it also returns the
same value or truth value. This completes the induction.
Theorem C.1 (Well-definedness). For every A ∈A,
JAK ∈O.
Proof. Fix A ∈A. We verify each condition in the definition of O.
Decision domain.
The Program production contains finitely many declarations and one
Objective. Its Set declarations define finite index sets, and its Parameter declarations define fixed
data. Each Variable declaration selects one of the permitted domains in Domain. Since there are
finitely many variables, these declarations determine a finitely presented decision domain
DA = D1 × · · · × Dn,
where every Di is binary, integer, real, bounded, or finite categorical. Each Piecewise declaration
has finitely many breakpoints and therefore defines a finitely presented piecewise-linear function.
Feasible set.
Let C1, . . . , Cq be the Constraint declarations in A. Each Cj contains a Formula;
by Lemma C.1, this formula returns a truth value for every valid x ∈DA. Let hj(x) denote that
value. The hard constraints therefore define the feasible set
FA = {x ∈DA : hj(x) = true for every j = 1, . . . , q}.
The same lemma ensures that each hj is constructed only from the expressions and conditions
permitted in O.
Base objective.
If the Objective contains an expression, Lemma C.1 implies that it defines a
scalar function f0 on DA. To express every objective as a minimization ordering, define
¯f0(x) =



f0(x),
if the sense is minimize,
−f0(x),
if the sense is maximize,
0,
if the sense is feasibility.
Thus, ¯f0 induces exactly the ordering specified by the Objective.
25


--- Page 26 ---
Soft constraints.
Let S1, . . . , Sm be the SoftConstraint declarations. By Lemma C.1, each
condition and guard is Boolean-valued and each explicit violation is a well-sorted expression. Under
the interpretation of SoftConstraint described above, these fields define a nonnegative violation
function vi on DA.
If the aggregation mode is weighted_sum, well-formedness supplies a nonnegative weight wi for
each vi. The program orders feasible solutions by the scalar function
¯f0(x) +
m
X
i=1
wivi(x),
which is a weighted-penalty objective of the form permitted in O.
If the aggregation mode is lexicographic, the priority fields and PreferenceRelation declara-
tions place the finitely many soft constraints into finitely many consistently ordered levels. Number
these levels from most to least important and define
Vk(x) =
X
i:Priority(i)=k
vi(x).
The program then orders feasible solutions lexicographically by
␀V1(x), . . . , VK(x), ¯f0(x)

,
which is a finite lexicographic objective of the form permitted in O. If A has no soft constraints, its
ordering is determined by ¯f0 alone.
Therefore, A defines a finitely presented problem with an admissible decision domain, a feasible
set defined by permitted conditions, and a base, weighted-penalty, or finite lexicographic objective.
Hence,
JAK ∈O.
Theorem C.2 (Expressive completeness). For every O ∈O, there exists A ∈A such that
JAK = O.
Proof. Fix O ∈O. We construct an AST A ∈A and show that it represents the same optimization
problem as O.
Decision domain.
Because O is finitely presented, it contains finitely many index domains, data
quantities, decision quantities, and piecewise-linear functions. Represent each finite index domain
by a Set declaration and each data quantity by a Parameter declaration with the same value and
domain. Represent each decision quantity by a Variable declaration with the same domain, indices,
and bounds. Represent each piecewise-linear function by a Piecewise declaration with the same
input, breakpoints, and values or marginal rates. These declarations reproduce the decision domain
DO of O.
Feasible set.
Let h1, . . . , hq be the hard constraints of O. By Lemma C.1, each hj has a Formula
representation bhj that returns the same truth value as hj for every valid assignment. Place each bhj in
a Constraint declaration. The resulting constraints define
{x ∈DO : bhj(x) = true for every j} = {x ∈DO : hj(x) = true for every j},
so they reproduce the feasible set of O.
Base objective.
If O has a base objective f0, Lemma C.1 supplies an Expr that returns f0(x)
for every valid assignment. Place this expression in an Objective with the same minimization
or maximization sense as O. If O is a feasibility problem, use feasibility with no objective
expression. The resulting Objective therefore reproduces the base ordering of O.
26


--- Page 27 ---
Soft constraints.
For each soft constraint i, use Lemma C.1 to represent its satisfaction condition
by a Formula and its nonnegative violation function vi by an Expr. Place these representations in
the condition and violation fields of a SoftConstraint declaration.
If O uses weighted penalties, set aggregation to weighted_sum and place the corresponding
nonnegative coefficient wi in weight. The resulting declarations reproduce the objective
¯f0(x) +
X
i
wivi(x).
If O uses lexicographic priorities, set aggregation to lexicographic and place the level of each
soft constraint in priority. When preference relations fully determine the ordered tiers, encode
the ordering with PreferenceRelation declarations. Otherwise, specify the tiers explicitly in
priority. These declarations reproduce the ordered objective vector
␀V1(x), . . . , VK(x), ¯f0(x)

,
Vk(x) =
X
i:Priority(i)=k
vi(x).
Assembly.
Collect the constructed declarations and objective in a Program. All components use
productions of G, and their types, domains, and aggregation fields agree with their declarations;
therefore, the resulting AST A belongs to A. Its declarations reproduce the decision domain of O, its
hard constraints reproduce the feasible set of O, and its objective and soft constraints reproduce the
ordering of feasible solutions in O. Under the stated notion of equivalence,
JAK = O.
Corollary C.1 (Representational adequacy). The semantic image of G is exactly O:
{JAK : A ∈A} = O.
Proof. Theorem C.1 gives the inclusion from left to right, and Theorem C.2 gives the reverse
inclusion.
D
Prompts and Inference Protocol
The following are the exact prompt templates used in the reported comparison. Text in double braces
is replaced deterministically before the request is sent.
D.1
ASTOR
AST prompt template
You are an expert in mathematical optimization. Your task is to formalize a
natural-language optimization problem as an optimization model.
You will be given a formal grammar that generates well-formed optimization
models. Using this grammar, construct an abstract syntax tree representing the
model the problem describes.
The problem may contain hard constraints, which
must always be satisfied, and soft constraints, which may be violated. It is
your job to determine the hardness or strength of each constraint, which may
be indicated by modal words of varied strength or by explicit comparison. For
problems with soft constraints, decide whether the optimization is
lexicographic or uses a weighted-sum penalty objective.
Here is the formal grammar:
{{grammar}}

The text inserted at

CoT compiler adapter
Compiler adapter: although the upstream prompt describes a callable function, this project executes

D.5
ORThought and Chain-of-Experts
Both multi-agent baselines run from their official implementations, ORThought at commit 5293e248
of its public repository [Yang et al., 2026] and Chain-of-Experts at commit afb89bf6 [Xiao et al.,
2024]. Their prompt prose is unchanged. Each agent prompt is followed by the same instance-data,
task-semantics, and compatibility contracts that Codegen receives, and the prompt that emits the final
program also carries the Codegen reporting protocol. ORThought runs its model agent once and then
up to three execution-conditioned debug rounds, which see only technical execution errors. CoE runs
the conductor over the seven upstream experts for three selections, then the reducer, with the optional
reflection pass disabled. Both use the backbone, decoding settings, and execution limits of Table 12,
so an ORThought attempt makes one to four LLM requests and a CoE attempt makes seven. The
verbatim prompt files and adaptation notes are in the released code.
D.6
Benchmark Contracts
Direct receives the task semantics only. ASTOR, Codegen, CoT, ORThought, and CoE also receive
the route-specific compatibility text. These are the exact strings used for the reported benchmarks.
Hard-constraint benchmarks
TASK SEMANTICS:
Enforce every required choice with an equality or an activated lower bound; an upper bound alone is
insufficient.
AST AND CODE COMPATIBILITY:
No benchmark-specific decision interface is required.
COMPASS
TASK SEMANTICS:
Select exactly one option. Report select[option_id] = 1 for the chosen option, using the supplied id
verbatim; omitted entries count as 0.
AST COMPATIBILITY:
Declare binary decision variable select indexed by [Options] and select exactly one option. Bind
every option-dependent soft-condition index within its formula.
CODE COMPATIBILITY:
30


--- Page 31 ---
Use Gurobi binary variables select[option] over Options and select exactly one option.
TravelPlanner
TASK SEMANTICS:
Select exactly one placement, one eligible transport option per leg, one eligible hotel per visited
city, and one eligible restaurant per active meal slot; selected restaurants must be distinct.
Evaluate preferences from most to least important; improvement on a less important preference
cannot compensate for worsening a more important one, and consider total cost only afterward.
Report the chosen plan as use_placement[placement_id], use_transport[transport_id], pick_hotel[
placement_id,hotel_id], and assign_meal[meal_slot_id,restaurant_id] entries set to 1, using
supplied ids verbatim; omitted entries count as 0.
AST COMPATIBILITY:
Candidate *_ok and *_active parameters define eligibility.
Use these binary decision variables exactly: use_placement[Placements], use_transport[
TransportOptions], pick_hotel[Placements,Hotels], and assign_meal[MealSlots,Restaurants].
CODE COMPATIBILITY:
Candidate *_ok and *_active parameters define eligibility.
Use these Gurobi binary variable families exactly: use_placement[placement], use_transport[option],
pick_hotel[placement,hotel], and assign_meal[slot,restaurant].
LexiBench
TASK SEMANTICS:
Enforce every required choice with an equality or an activated lower bound; an upper bound alone is
insufficient. Evaluate preferences from most to least important; improvement on a less important
preference cannot compensate for worsening a more important one, and apply any stated tie-break
only afterward. Report exactly one indexed decision-variable family per supplied set, including
every member with unselected members set to 0; report no auxiliary quantities.
AST COMPATIBILITY:
No benchmark-specific decision interface is required.
CODE COMPATIBILITY:
Create each decision-variable family with model.addVars(members, vtype=..., name="family") so Gurobi
formats the brackets; never build a name with an f-string like f"family_{member}".
Nurse Rostering
TASK SEMANTICS:
Minimize the combined penalty for staffing-target deviations and unmet shift requests according to
their stated severities. Report work[nurse,day,shift] = 1 for every worked shift, using supplied
ids verbatim; omitted entries count as 0. Any numerical penalties you choose to use must be
inferred from text and instantiated yourself. Never invent other problem data.
AST COMPATIBILITY:
Declare binary decision variable work indexed by [Nurses,Days,Shifts], where 1 means the nurse works
that shift on that day. Auxiliary variables may use arbitrary names.
Declare every set and parameter listed in the external data contract exactly once, using those exact
names and index domains, with values provided in EXTERNAL DATA CONTRACT declared null. You must
instantiate any penalty weights with numbers or expressions.
CODE COMPATIBILITY:
Create work = model.addVars(nurses, days, shifts, vtype=GRB.BINARY, name="work"), where 1 means the
nurse works that shift on that day. Auxiliary variables may use arbitrary names.
For schema-bearing AST instances other than Nurse Rostering, the following sentence is appended
verbatim to the AST compatibility contract:
External-data binding
Declare every set and parameter listed in the external data contract exactly once, using those exact
names and index domains, with null external values.
The instance-data contract in Codegen and CoT states that INSTANCE_DATA is a flat dictionary with no
sets or parameters wrapper. For schema-bearing instances, sets are lists, indexed parameters use
31


--- Page 32 ---
string or comma-joined keys, and scalar parameters are bare numbers. For prose-only instances, the
contract states verbatim: “INSTANCE_DATA is an empty dict for this problem:
every
value you need is stated in the problem text itself.”
D.7
Execution and Evaluation
ASTOR makes one LLM request. The output includes exactly one JSON block, repaired deter-
ministically only when JSON syntax admits an unambiguous local correction, checked against the
response schema and symbol table, and compiled deterministically to Gurobi. Direct is evaluated
from its reported assignment; Codegen and CoT execute their single returned Python program, and
ORThought and CoE execute the final program returned by their last agent. All routes then use the
same benchmark oracle. The frozen runs contain 790 scored ASTOR attempts and no JSON-repair,
error-retry, or rephrase API call artifacts; thus each scored ASTOR attempt used one LLM request.
For numeric objectives, a prediction is correct when the solver reports the gold status and the absolute
error is at most max{10−4, 10−5 max(1, |z⋆|)}, where z⋆is the gold-standard optimal objective
value for the instance. Infeasible and unbounded gold outcomes require an exact status match.
Soft benchmarks additionally decode the reported assignment, verify feasibility, and recompute the
weighted penalty or lexicographic tier vector; a lexicographic result must match every tier and its
final numeric tie-break.
Table 12: Frozen settings for the main experiment.
Setting
Value

Gemini 3.7 Flash; Nurse Rostering: Gemini 3.8 Flash

Temperature 0; maximum output 32,768 tokens (65,536 for Nurse

Nurse Rostering is the one exception to the default thinking configuration. Under the provider default,
all routes had substantial difficulty with Nurse Rostering, so the reported Nurse Rostering runs use a
higher thinking budget and token limit for all six routes.
D.8
Ablation Definitions
The component study changes one element of the full ASTOR condition at a time, holding the main
experimental setup constant. Without benchmark contract replaces both benchmark-contract fields by
None.; and without deterministic repair disables local JSON repair while leaving the model request
unchanged. Direct + AST is a prompt-only control rather than an ASTOR variant: the Direct prompt
with the ASTOR grammar of Appendix C prepended and an instruction to construct the abstract
syntax tree of the model as an internal reasoning step before answering. Its output schema, benchmark
contract, instance data, decoding settings, and evaluation are those of Direct, and nothing is compiled
or solved.
D.9
Frozen Ablation Sample
Following the cost-controlled analyses in NEMO, OptMATH, and SeaKR, which use restricted
benchmark sets or sampled analysis subsets, we run ablations on a frozen subset of the main
32


--- Page 33 ---
evaluation cohort [Song et al., 2026, Lu et al., 2025, Yao et al., 2025]. We use Hamilton largest-
remainder allocation to assign exactly 100 of the 790 instances proportionally across the eight reported
benchmarks, yielding 55 hard-constraint and 45 soft-constraint instances [Balinski and Young, 2001].
With master seed 20260825, we sample uniformly without replacement within each stratum; the
COMPASS allocation is further divided proportionally into ten hotel and one complex instance. The
same IDs are used for every ablation condition, and no method output is used in their selection.

D.10
Artifact Index
The anonymous repository contains the complete grammar and its JSON schema, the exact prompt
templates for every method and for the Direct + AST control, the frozen 100-instance ablation
manifest, the contract-construction code, the parser, validator, and compiler, the benchmark adapters
and evaluators together with the SoftOR data, the frozen experiment configurations, the per-problem
result records of the 790-instance evaluation and of the backbone ablation, the reporting inputs from
which every table and figure is regenerated, and the test suite.
E
Error Annotations and Discussion
For the error analysis in the main text, errors are classified as follows: a recorded parser, compiler,
solver-execution, or other harness failure is technical. This includes a non-successful formulation-
conversion status. An attempt that passes the automatic evaluator is correct. Every remaining attempt
is a solution error. Thus the error rates use all evaluated attempts as their denominator, and the
unplotted remainder in Figures 3b and 7 is correct.
For example, ComplexOR prob_007 under Codegen returned no Python fence and was labeled
technical. ComplexOR prob_008 under CoT executed normally but returned objective 10 against
gold 7 and was labeled a solution error.
E.1
Additional Error Analysis
E.1.1
Soft Constraints
On LexiBench, ASTOR returns hard-feasible solutions on all 75 instances, but six have incorrect
preference outcomes. Five of these use weighted-sum aggregation with a cost objective, while the
sixth assigns higher priority to preferences that the request explicitly says to sacrifice first. Among the
local constraints in the 180 evaluated TravelPlanner instances, ASTOR treats 17 of 124 preferences
as hard constraints and 5 of 116 hard constraints as preferences. Treating a preference as hard was
harmless in 11 of the 17 cases, and treating a hard constraint as a preference never caused a failure.
ASTOR has 41 unsuccessful attempts on SoftOR: 27 on TravelPlanner, 6 on LexiBench, 7 on Nurse
Rostering, and 1 on COMPASS. Of these, 1 is a technical failure and 40 are classified as solution
errors by the evaluator. All seven unsuccessful Nurse Rostering attempts return hard-feasible rosters,
with published-weight penalties between 1 and 4 points above the gold optimum. Lexicographic
mistakes include wrong preference tiers or misdiagnosing a soft constraint as hard. Some examples:
In the laptop instance, five equal wishes are followed by “the cheaper one wins”; ASTOR kept all five
wishes but summed them with price, and satisfied three instead of four. In the service-vehicle instance,
the text ranks wishes as “we would sooner run without X than without Y ”; ASTOR reversed the
33


--- Page 34 ---
order. In the makerspace instance, the top wish is “the one thing we will not trade”; ASTOR made it
a hard constraint.
When a method gets a soft-constraint problem wrong, it is usually not because it missed a preference.
It often treats one preference as too strict, or mixes the preferences together the wrong way. The
baselines often end up minimizing cost instead of respecting the priority order, so a cheap plan wins
even when it skips something more important. ASTOR’s mistakes go the other way: it sometimes
turns a preference into a hard rule, or lets cost outweigh a preference it should have kept.
E.1.2
Hard Constraints
On the hard-constraint benchmarks, a wrong answer is almost always a wrong objective value rather
than a failed solve. A value better than gold means the method was able to achieve a lower value
for a minimization objective or a higher value for a maximization objective than the annotated
gold-standard optimum, and a value worse than gold means the opposite. Dropped constraints are
the more common error for every method, by about two to one: Codegen returns 47 values better
than gold and 22 worse, CoT 51 and 23, ORThought 55 and 22, CoE 46 and 24, and ASTOR 43 and
17, the fewest over-constrained formulations. Direct, which solves by hand, returns 71 better and 31
worse. Infeasible or unbounded formulations are rare, at most 3 per method.
When a method gets a hard-constraint problem wrong, it is almost always because it left out a
constraint, not because it added one that was not there. That makes the solver report a better answer
than is actually allowed. It is rare for a method to end up with an infeasible or over-constrained
model instead. The grammar does not stop constraints from getting dropped, but when one does get
dropped, it is more likely to show up as an obvious error instead of a wrong answer that looks right.

F.1
TravelPlanner Priority Rules
TravelPlanner uses modal language to distinguish requirements from preferences. We map deontic,
teleological, and bouletic expressions to three optimization levels [Rubinstein et al., 2013, von Fintel
and Iatridou, 2008, Portner, 2009, Henning et al., 2022].
Table 15: TravelPlanner modal priority rules.
Tier
Interpretation
Common cues
1
Hard constraint
must, require, need, essential, mandatory, cannot, non-
negotiable, ensure, will not, do not plan, avoid, not via
2
Strong preference
should, important, intend to, plan to, aiming for
3
Weak preference
prefer, would like, appreciate, hope, wish, interested in, ideally,
open to, prefer not, rather not
Budget, party size, origin, destination, and the original TravelPlanner validity rules are always hard
constraints. Other local constraints are classified using the modal cue in the same clause. Tier 1 takes
precedence when several cues match, except that prefer not and rather not remain weak preferences.
Unrecognized expressions default to Tier 3 and are flagged for review. This procedure recognizes a
cue for all 180 instances used in our experiments.
Let x range over candidate plans, let vi(x) ∈{0, 1} indicate that plan x violates local constraint i,
let Priority(i) ∈{1, 2} be its strong or weak tier (tiers 2 and 3 of Table 15; tier 1 becomes a hard
constraint hj), and let f0(x) be the plan’s cost. The gold objective is
lex min
x
␀V1(x), V2(x), f0(x)


hj(x) ≤0
∀j,

X
i:Priority(i)=k
vi(x).
A prediction is correct if it attains the same objective vector as the gold plan. It need not select the
same plan when several plans are optimal.
The original TravelPlanner authors created 225 total instances, which together have 300 hard and soft
constraints. We only use 180 of these instances (the subset they labeled "validation"), which together
have 240 hard and soft constraints.
F.2

LexiBench contains five instances for every combination of three decision types and five preference
structures, giving 3 × 5 × 5 = 75 problems.

possible combinations.

Hard
LexiBench uses the same modal words in Table 15 to signal preferences, with the same tier structure.
It also uses explicit words "more important," "less important," and "above all" to get more than three
tiers.
Difficulty depends only on preference structure, not decision type. The benchmark therefore contains
30 easy, 15 medium, and 30 hard problems. These labels and the gold annotations are not shown to
the model.
Let vi(x) ∈{0, 1} indicate that decision x violates preference i, let Priority(i) be its annotated level,
ordered from highest to lowest, and let f0(x) be the stated tie-break objective, omitted when none
is stated. Hard constraints hj come from budget, capacity, or required attributes marked by deontic
language in the natural language instance. The gold objective is
lex min

∀j,

i:Priority(i)=k
vi(x).
We certify each gold vector with Gurobi. We optimize the highest preference level, fix its optimal
value, and repeat for each lower level. Any ordinary objective or tie-break is optimized last. Every
stage must be optimal with zero MIP gap. A frozen manifest records the build seed, benchmark hash,
solver version, and successful verification of all 75 problems.
F.3
Nurse Rostering
We convert the published request weights into qualitative language.
Table 18: Nurse Rostering preference phrases.
Published weight
Natural-language phrase
1
slightly prefers
2
prefers
3
strongly prefers
100
far more serious
The included instances assign penalties of 100 to understaffing and 1 to overstaffing. We express
this by stating that understaffing is “far more serious” than overstaffing. The numerical penalties are
not shown to the model and are only used to evaluate the final roster produced by each method. If
the route chooses to use weights in creating a roster, it must create its own weights. Once the roster
is produced, we only use the original numerical penalties for evaluation, but they are never used in
generating a solution.
Note that the request weights 1, 2, 3, 100 are the numbers chosen by the original authors of Nurse
Rostering at SchedulingBenchmarks, but those numbers are not unique in determining the preference
order. For example, 3, 14, 86, and 1592 would create the same ordering. As a result, for our newly
constructed natural language instances which only signal request strength through linguistic cues, it is
precisely the task of each method to be able to infer and instantiate numerical weights which reflect
the strength of the given language. In the weighted penalty experiments we never show the original
weights of 1, 2, 3, 100 to the models, and allow them to choose their own numbers or whether to use
weights at all. After doing this, they will produce a nurse roster for this problem, which specifies
which nurses work on which days using indicator decision variables. We only use the original weights
1, 2, 3, 100 after the decision is made for the sake of evaluation: to accrue the penalty of each roster
by noting when the chosen decision violates staffing and shift preferences, and multiplying by their
weights in accordance with the original SchedulingBenchmarks gold-standard calculation.
36


--- Page 37 ---
Let xnds ∈{0, 1} indicate that nurse n works shift s on day d, and let rds be the number of
nurses required on day d and shift s, as specified by the instance’s cover requirement for each
(d, s) ∈{days} × {shifts}. Each shift request i names a nurse, day, and shift (ni, di, si) together
with the phrase that carries its weight. The gold roster solves the weighted-penalty problem
min
x
V1(x) + 2 V2(x) + 3 V3(x) + 100 U(x) + O(x)
s.t.
hj(x) ≤0
∀j,

(d,s)
␀requiredds −assignedds(x)
+,
Overstaffing:
O(x) = P
(d,s)
␀assignedds(x) −requiredds
+,
where (·)+ = max{0, ·}, the sums run over days d and shifts s, requiredds = rds, assignedds(x) =
P
n xnds, and the hard constraints hj encode the scheduling rules of the source benchmark. Vk(x)
counts the violated requests phrased slightly prefers (k = 1), prefers (k = 2), and strongly prefers
(k = 3); a request to work a shift is violated when the nurse is not assigned to it, and a request not to
work a shift is violated when the nurse is. This is the weighted-penalty form of Section 3.1 with no
base objective: request weights 1, 2, 3, understaffing weight 100, and overstaffing weight 1. Each
predicted roster is checked against the original hard scheduling rules described below and rescored
using this objective. The published optimal objective is used as the gold value.
Table 19 reports partial-credit measures. Hard Constraints Satisfied is calculated separately for
each roster. Each nurse is evaluated on nine hard constraint categories, which form the hj in the
formulation above: at most one shift per day, forbidden shift successions, limits on assignments
to each shift type, total working-time bounds, fixed days off, maximum consecutive working days,
minimum consecutive working days, minimum consecutive days off, and maximum weekends worked.
A nurse receives one point for a category if and only if the rule is satisfied throughout the planning
horizon. The roster score is the percentage of all nurse–category pairs receiving one point. Following
the benchmark, blocks extending beyond the start or end of the horizon are excluded from the two
minimum-consecutive-length checks.
The remaining measures are also calculated separately for each roster:
Understaffing = missing required nurse–shift positions
total required nurse–shift positions .
Overstaffing = assignments above staffing requirements
total required nurse–shift positions
.
Weighted Preference Violation = total weight of violated shift requests
total weight of all shift requests
.
Understaffing and overstaffing may both be nonzero because different shifts can fall below and exceed
their requirements. Table 19 reports the complements of these three measures, so that higher is
better in every column: staffing coverage is one minus understaffing or overstaffing, and weighted
preference satisfied is one minus weighted preference violation. Each of the 15 instances receives
equal weight in its method’s reported average, and an attempt with no decodable roster counts as
satisfying no constraint.

Direct returned five evaluable rosters: two satisfied all hard constraints and three violated at least

Working-time, consecutive-working-day, consecutive-days-off, weekend, and shift-count limits were

Currently, the version of Nurse Rostering we use has each route infer and instantiate its own penalty
weights, and only uses author-published weights for calculating penalties for the final scoring. We
chose this setup because our main question is whether methods can turn natural-language preferences
into decisions. Supplying the numerical weights before optimization would provide part of the
preference interpretation that we want the methods to perform. As an ablation, we ran a version
of Nurse Rostering that allowed methods to see weights before decision-making, using the same
experimental settings as the main Nurse Rostering experiment. Direct sees numerical weights
associated with natural language directly in the prompt, and all other routes use variable placeholders
for each weight, which are deterministically replaced with the actual weights 1, 2, 3, or 100 when the
code is generated, before running it to find an optimal solution. The results are presented in the Table
21, which should be read in the same way as Table 4.
The task-semantics contract for this supplied-weight setting is reproduced verbatim below.
Nurse Rostering with supplied weights: task-semantics contract
Minimize the combined penalty for staffing-target deviations and unmet shift requests according to
their stated severities. Report work[nurse,day,shift] = 1 for every worked shift, using supplied
ids verbatim; omitted entries count as 0.

Supplying the numerical weights removes the need to infer preference strength, but still requires
translating the scheduling rules into a valid executable formulation. Nurse rostering is still challenging
in this setting: some methods violate hard constraints or fail to return an evaluable roster consistently.
F.4
COMPASS
We convert each structured COMPASS record into natural language using fixed templates. Hard
constraints begin with:
The following conditions are required:
Soft constraints begin with:
The following wishes are preferred but not required, and all are equally important:
Each requirement and wish is rendered as a numbered sentence. The generated text is parsed back
into structured form to verify that no constraint was changed or omitted.
38


--- Page 39 ---
Let x range over the supplied candidates, let vi(x) ∈{0, 1} indicate that candidate x fails wish i, and
let the requirements be the hard constraints hj(x) ≤0 (marked in the instance with “require"). All
wishes share one priority level, so the gold objective is
lex min
x
␀V1(x)

s.t.
hj(x) ≤0
∀j,
V1(x) =
X
i
vi(x).
We recompute the optimum over all candidates and accept any feasible choice that attains it, including
ties absent from the original annotation.
F.5
ORThought Gold-Label Corrections
We found 16 ORThought records whose answer files reported an optimal status but contained no
objective value [Yang et al., 2026]. We retained the original problem statements and reference
formulations, reran the bundled solver code, and updated only the missing gold outcome. For solver
results initially reported as infeasible or unbounded, we disabled dual reductions to distinguish the
two statuses.

F.6
ComplexOR Key-Name Reconciliation
Eight of ComplexOR’s [Xiao et al., 2024] eighteen problems describe their data using one set of
symbols in the natural-language question and another in the accompanying instance JSON. We
reconciled the two representations by renaming each instance-JSON key to the symbol the question
text uses for it.
